title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most C·ε^{−c} vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let P_F contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define dist(G,P_F) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in P_F on the same vertex set, divided by n²; define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of min{n,s} distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when G[S] contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers C,c≥1 such that for every rational ε∈(0,1), every n≥1 and every G with dist(G,P_F)>ε, this tester with s=⌈Cε^{−c}⌉ rejects with probability at least 2/3. It automatically accepts every graph in P_F. The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy ε are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove decidability by giving a terminating, correct classification procedure for all finite forbidden families, or prove that no such procedure exists. This is an explicit effective version of the source’s broader structural-classification problem. A criterion that still quantifies over all host graphs and all accuracies does not establish decidability unless those conditions can themselves be decided from the finite family. Classifying only single forbidden graphs or a restricted family is partial progress.
context:
The source survey asks for a characterization of finite forbidden-induced-subgraph families whose canonical sample complexity is polynomial in inverse accuracy. To make the requested output unambiguous, this card fixes an effective classification question: can that class of finite inputs be decided at all? This additional effectiveness requirement is an editorial specification, rather than wording attributed to the survey. It distinguishes the target from an equivalent reformulation involving another unresolved infinite condition.

There are two separate computational tasks. Given a fixed family F and a particular finite graph, exact membership in P_F can be checked by searching for its finitely many forbidden patterns. The question here concerns a statement about every possible host graph and arbitrarily small ε. Finite decidability of each individual membership test does not by itself provide a decision procedure for the existence of uniform polynomial sampling bounds.

The dense-model normalization matters. Being ε-far means that a positive ε fraction of all possible vertex pairs must be changed, up to the fixed normalization factor. It does not mean that an ε fraction of the edges currently present must be removed. A sparse graph can therefore be close to a property even when many of its own edges would need modification. No bounded-degree or sparse-input model is implicit.

One-sided error gives rejection a concrete witness: the sampled vertices contain a forbidden induced graph. For an induced copy, both edges and nonedges must agree with the pattern. Thus a four-clique contains an ordinary four-cycle as a subgraph, but no induced four-cycle. Replacing induced copies with arbitrary copies changes the classification problem substantially.

The general hereditary testing theorem guarantees some sample bound depending only on ε, but that bound can be much larger than every polynomial. For finite F, inspecting all pairs in a sample squares its size, which preserves the distinction between polynomial and nonpolynomial dependence. Since F is fixed during testing, exhaustive checking inside the sample also has a fixed polynomial exponent, although that exponent need not be uniform across families.

Gishboliner–Shapira prove a useful sufficient condition: a finite family containing a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph is polynomially testable. Here co-bipartite means a union of two cliques, and split means a partition into a clique and an independent set; the three roles may be played by the same graph. Their necessary condition requires a bipartite and a co-bipartite member, but this is not sufficient.

The gap between these conditions is real. There are finite families containing a bipartite and a co-bipartite graph that are not polynomially testable. Conversely, split graphs themselves form a polynomially testable class, described by forbidding C₄, its complement and C₅, although none of those forbidden graphs is split. Thus simply promoting either known condition to an equivalence would give wrong answers on known examples.

Even a singleton family remains instructive. Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, which are precisely graphs with no induced four-vertex path.

Induced C₄-freeness and its complement remain the exceptional cases identified in the 2025 survey.

Gishboliner–Shapira obtain a single-exponential sample bound for induced C₄-freeness; that improves substantially on regularity-based bounds but is not polynomial in 1/ε.

An August 2026 preprint by Carenini–Seth–Yoshida gives a new quantitative characterization using ordered containers. Roughly, property-satisfying induced subgraphs inside a graph far from the property must fit into smaller vertex sets determined by short fingerprints. Theorem 1.4 translates between tester bounds and these container parameters by explicit polynomial transformations. This is relevant new progress beyond the survey.

Its effectiveness has a specific meaning: given suitable quantitative bounds on one side, the theorem supplies bounds on the other. The container premise still ranges over all sufficiently large host graphs and all accuracy parameters. The inspected theorem does not give a terminating procedure that takes only F and decides whether polynomial container parameters exist. It therefore does not establish the effective finite-family classification asked here.

The distinction is useful independently of how the eventual classification looks. An affirmative answer would provide a finite method for recognizing when global violations must have abundant small witnesses. An undecidability theorem would show that no universal terminating rule can perform this recognition from arbitrary finite forbidden lists, even though each list defines a straightforward graph-membership problem. Either outcome would identify a fundamental limit of turning qualitative testing theorems into systematic algorithm design.
why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

importance.reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.

progress.text: Alon–Shapira establish one-sided testability for all hereditary graph properties, without a general polynomial bound.
Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability of induced-P₄-freeness, the cograph case.
Gishboliner–Shapira develop sufficient and necessary forbidden-family conditions, with a STOC 2017 precursor and IMRN 2021 publication.
A single-exponential bound is obtained for induced-C₄ removal; polynomial dependence remains a separate target.
The Polynomial Property Testing survey states the finite-family classification as Problem 3.14.
ECCC publishes the quantitative ordered-container characterization; its parameter conversion does not supply a finite-family decision procedure.
